8ballpool · ai/policy.py

Watch the AI decide

It is not a neural network — there are no layers to draw. It is a search running in three passes: throw out every pot the geometry says is impossible, play every surviving idea out under the real physics, and score each outcome on thirteen weighted terms. Below is one decision, slowed down enough to follow. The rolling is the simulation the search itself ran, sampled every fifth frame — click any candidate to replay that shot instead.

Phase 1 · costs almost nothing

Throw out the impossible

It takes one ball it is allowed to hit, asks it against all six pockets, then moves to the next ball. Each question needs the ghost ball: the spot the cue ball must arrive at to send that ball at that pocket. So each question is really two runs — the cue ball's run to the ghost spot, and the ball's run to the pocket — and it survives only if both are clear and the cut is not so thin the contact would barely move the ball. No physics runs here; it is arithmetic on straight lines, which is why it can afford to ask about everything.

On the table: the ball being asked about is ringed, and so is the cue ball. Each question draws a dashed leg from the cue ball to the ghost circle, a leg from there on to the pocket, and the cut angle where they meet — whichever part fails turns red. When the ball is done its fan is wiped, and only the pots that survived stay.
Phase 2 · nearly all of the time

Play every idea out

Each surviving pot turns into several candidates — the straight pot, the same pot aimed a hair either side, harder, softer, and struck off centre for spin — joined by cushion banks, deliberate safeties and a few random probes so it is never blind. Every one is then actually played: the same physics and the same rulebook as the game you play, run until the last ball stops. The position it leaves is scored on thirteen weighted terms, and only the total is compared.

On the table: one ray per candidate out of the cue ball — direction is the aim, length is the power, colour is the score, dark green highest. The balls jump to where that candidate leaves them.
Phase 3 · what you see in the game

Play the best one

The highest total wins, that shot is played, and every other candidate is discarded without ever being shown to you. Here it is replayed ball by ball, a little slower than it happens, with its thirteen terms filling in underneath as it rolls. Click any other candidate — in the strip or the list — to replay that shot instead and see what it would have been worth.

On the table: the blue trail is the cue ball's path, the dashed outlines are where every ball ends up, and the dashed blue ring is the leave the AI was playing for.

The thirteen weights — the whole of what it values

Every number and every frame came out of the game itself: python -m ai.inspect --out ai_decisions.json replays each position through the real PhysicsEngine and RulesEngine, sampling ball positions every five frames.

The one thing worth distrusting is position_reward. It is fed by a single number — the difficulty of the easiest pot left on the table — which cannot see a cluster, a blocker, or whether the ball after the next one has an angle. Ten hours of training cut that weight to a fifth of its old size: the optimiser worked out on its own that the term carries almost no signal.
